{#zbmb} ## Prevalence of anemia among HIV positive children at KRRH

{#uz1z} Regarding, the prevalence, 57.3% of the participants had anemia, which was predominantly moderate according to severity with Microcytosis and hypochromia. This prevalence was high. This high prevalence can be explained by the low social economic status of the participants as shown by the family monthly income, which was less than 200,000 in over 50% of the participants (Table 1). The low income might be affecting the feeding practices, resulting in nutritional deficiencies [@w:w10]. These nutritional deficiencies can often contribute to the anemia [@w:w11], as seen in this study where stunting and wasting all had a significant association with anemia.

{#wvsn} It is also important to note that, undernutrition is often associated with micronutrient deficiencies [@w:w12]. This can be affirmed by the fact that majority of the participates in the current study had microcytic anemia (Table 3), whose main etiology is Iron deficiency. Another indicator of low social economic status is the education level, where over 70% of the caretakers either never had a formal education or only had a primary education (Table 1). The low education level generally affects the financial status as well as the understandingin regard to the care and nutrition of children. The poor social economic status can also result in comorbidities like intestinal warms w

ops.markdown: Undernutrition is also often associated with micronutrient deficiencies [@w:w12], consistent with most participants in this study having microcytic anemia (Table 3), whose main etiology is iron deficiency. Education level is another indicator of low socioeconomic status: over 70% of caretakers had no formal education or only primary education (Table 1), which affects financial status and understanding of child care and nutrition. Poor socioeconomic status may also lead to comorbidities such as intestinal worms, causing recurrent blood loss and anemia, as reported by [@w:w13] in Ethiopia.
